Holistic balance: how evenly wellness is held across the domains of a whole person

Source: R/igm.R
holbal.Rd

For each group, from published percentages of wellness in each holistic domain (physical, emotional, mental, spiritual, or the domains a community names), the overall level of wellness and how balanced it is across the domains, with Monte Carlo intervals from the published ones.

Usage

holbal(
  data,
  grp,
  domain,
  est,
  lower,
  upper,
  w = NULL,
  qual = NULL,
  reps = 10000,
  seed = 1,
  conflvl = 0.95
)

Arguments

data

A data frame, one row per group and indicator (as scests gives).

grp, domain, est, lower, upper

Column names: the group, the domain of the indicator (any set of domains: Medicine Wheel, Te Whare Tapa Wha, a Nation's own), the percentage of wellness (0 to 100, strictly inside; multiply proportions by 100) and its published limits.

w

Optional named weights, one per domain (they are rescaled to sum to one).

qual

Optional column of quality flags for the estimates.

reps

Monte Carlo draws for the intervals (default 10,000).

seed

Seed for the draws, so the intervals are reproducible (default 1).

conflvl

Confidence level of the balance intervals (default 0.95).

Value

A data frame of class holbal: group, level, lvllo, lvlup, balance, ballo, balup, weadom, usewithcau; the attributes domains (the matrix of domain levels, groups by domains) and weights.

Details

Indigenous understandings of mental health are holistic: wellness is a balance among the domains of a person, and illness a loss of that balance (Stewart 2008; Gabriel, Mirza and Stewart 2022). A single indicator, or an average of indicators, cannot show balance: a group with 80% in two domains and 20% in two others has the same average as one with 50% in all four. This method, which is ours and inspired by that work rather than taken from it, measures balance as the ratio of the weighted geometric to the weighted arithmetic mean of the domain levels \(p_k\): $$B = \exp\left(\sum_k w_k \log p_k\right) / \sum_k w_k p_k,$$ one less Atkinson's (1970) index with inequality aversion 1. \(B = 1\) exactly when every domain with a positive weight is at the same level, and it falls toward 0 as one domain falls behind the others; it does not depend on the overall level, which is reported beside it (level, \(\sum_k w_k p_k\)) with the weakest domain.

The weights w say how much each domain counts. They are equal by default; a community that holds its own view of the domains sets its own (the CARE principle of authority to control, Carroll et al. 2020), and the result says which weights it used.

Several indicators in one domain are averaged, their standard errors combined as independent (they come from the same respondents, so that standard error is too small). The interval for \(B\) comes from reps draws of every domain level from a normal distribution on the logit scale with the standard error of its published interval, the domains independent. \(B\) is at most 1 and reaches 1 only at equal levels, so noise in the levels tends to pull the draws below \(\hat B\) (\(B\) is not concave; the direction of the bias is seen in the draws, not guaranteed): the percentile interval is shifted back by the draws' mean bias (\(\bar B^* - \hat B\)), kept inside \((0, 1]\) and widened if need be to contain \(\hat B\). The level's interval is normal. A group with a suppressed or missing domain, or one whose published interval misses its own estimate, has no balance: the domain is not imputed.

What the domains mean, and which indicators stand for each, is for the communities to say; the published tables have few measures of spiritual wellness, and a domain with no fitting indicator should be left out rather than filled with another.

Acknowledgement

This estimator puts to quantitative use the framework of Professor Suzanne Stewart (Yellowknives Dene First Nation, University of Toronto).

See the acknowledgements in the section on Indigenous health of the package's vignette (vignette("crimlab")).

References

Atkinson AB (1970). On the measurement of inequality. Journal of Economic Theory 2(3):244-263. doi:10.1016/0022-0531(70)90039-6

Carroll SR, Garba I, Figueroa-Rodriguez OL, et al. (2020). The CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance. Data Science Journal 19:43. doi:10.5334/dsj-2020-043

Gabriel MD, Mirza S, Stewart SL (2022). Exploring mental health and holistic healing through the life stories of Indigenous youth who have experienced homelessness. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 19(20):13402. doi:10.3390/ijerph192013402

Stewart SL (2008). Promoting Indigenous mental health: cultural perspectives on healing from Native counsellors in Canada. International Journal of Health Promotion and Education 46(2):49-56. doi:10.1080/14635240.2008.10708129

See also

welprof, dualcont.

Examples

# your own table: made-up percentages of wellness in four domains a Nation
# set for itself, for two communities
own <- data.frame(
  community = rep(c("Lakeside", "Riverbend"), each = 4),
  domain = rep(c("body", "mind", "spirit", "family"), 2),
  pct = c(62, 58, 70, 75, 55, 61, 66, 80),
  lo = c(57, 53, 65, 70, 49, 55, 60, 75),
  hi = c(67, 63, 75, 80, 61, 67, 72, 85)
)
holbal(own, "community", "domain", "pct", "lo", "hi", reps = 2000)
#> Holistic balance across the domains
#> -----------------------------------
#> Groups:  2
#> Weights: equal, over 4 domains
#> Balance: weighted geometric over arithmetic mean of the domain levels
#> 
#>     group  level      level CI  balance      balance CI  weakest
#>  Lakeside  66.25  [63.7, 68.8]   0.9950   [0.99, 0.998]     mind
#> Riverbend  65.50  [62.6, 68.4]   0.9905  [0.984, 0.996]     body
#> 
#> Domain levels (percent)
#>     group  body  mind  spirit  family
#>  Lakeside    62    58      70      75
#> Riverbend    55    61      66      80
#> 
#> Highest balance: Lakeside (0.995); lowest: Riverbend (0.9905).
#> Their intervals overlap, which alone does not mean they are the same: the difference has its own, narrower interval.
#> The weakest domain is body for 1 of 2 groups.
#> 
#> balance is 1 when every domain is at the same level and falls toward
#> 0 as one falls behind; level is the weighted mean, reported beside it.
#> A method inspired by Stewart (2008), not taken from it.
#> The weights say how much each domain counts; a community may set
#> its own (CARE: authority to control, Carroll et al. 2020).
